summary.text:
A short annual report from a district-plus-HRA council with a debt book that has been running off and an investment book that has grown to sit against it. External borrowing fell from £236.238m to £208.519m during 2025/26 with no new external drawdown (§1.12), while investments rose from £92m to £142.428m. The over-borrowing position — external debt sitting above CFR — has been unwound from about £32.7m to £2.8m in a single year.

The paper prints no PWLB loan-book table and no maturity profile of borrowing, so a full loan-level reconciliation is not possible from this document. Our file holds 18 PWLB loans totalling £192,019,000 at a weighted 2.3743%, and the £192,019k in the Prudential Indicators Budget/Estimate column ties to that to the pound. The Actual line is £16.5m higher, presumably non-PWLB debt outside our file.

The investment side is the more distinctive shape. £83m across seventeen fixed-term deposits, placed entirely with UK local authorities from Eastleigh at 4.10% to Wrexham at 4.70%, weighted about 4.42% — no MMFs, no bank deposits, no corporate paper on the fixed-term side. Bank Rate ended the year at 3.75% (§1.9), so the LA-to-LA book was carrying about 67 basis points of premium over base at the fixings. A separate £59.428m sits with SAIL, a Council-owned entity.

Nothing here trips a distress or watch signal. Members are asked to recommend approval to Council on 15 September 2026.

officer.subject: Your £192,019k Budget/Estimate line ties to our record of your PWLB book exactly
officer.body:
Hi Sam,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts on the Treasury Annual Report that went to Audit, Governance and Standards on 28 July, ahead of Council on 15 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report is short and clean, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

A cross-check first. We hold 18 PWLB loans for Brentwood totalling £192,019,000 at a weighted 2.3743%, and the £192,019k in your Budget/Estimate column on page 5 ties to that to the pound. Your Actual line is £16,500k higher — non-PWLB we don't hold and the paper doesn't decompose. So the tie is to the estimate rather than the outturn, but the number we can price is the number you set the year against.

That book is legacy money and it looks it. The 2.37% average sits well below a Bank Rate that ended the year at 3.75%, and on today's DMO curve fifteen of the eighteen loans price below par with a substantial indicative discount across the file. Your report does not discuss premature repayment, so this is context rather than a suggestion, and any real settlement is the DMO's quote alone — we do not model MRP or any accounting treatment.

The other side of your balance sheet is the more distinctive shape. £83m of fixed-term investments placed entirely with UK local authorities across seventeen lines, weighted about 4.42%, running from Eastleigh at 4.10% out to Wrexham at 4.70%. No MMFs, no bank deposits, no corporate paper on the fixed-term side — two Liverpool lines and fifteen single-line exposures. Against 3.75% Bank Rate at year end that is about 67 basis points of premium over base at the fixings.

Which is why I'd point you to pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. The monthly sector data captures the borrower side of the market you're on the lending side of. Across everything we've read, LA borrowing has priced from about 4.15% at the tight end (Gloucestershire's £55m) out to 8.50% at the wide end (Cornwall for four days) — a four-hundred-basis-point range in one market that no single lender sees from its own trades.

One arithmetic note that isn't in the paper. Between 24/25 and 25/26 external borrowing fell from £236.238m to £208.519m, a £27.7m run-off, while investments rose from £92m to £142.428m. Against a CFR of £205.766m and effectively no long-term liabilities (§1.19 puts leases at £22k, all short-term), external borrowing at year end sits £2.753m above CFR — a year earlier that gap was £32.715m. The over-borrowing position has been substantially unwound in the year with no new external drawdown.

None of this needs a meeting or a subscription, and the rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds to check. On training, four look most relevant to Brentwood: Interest rate risk, for a 2.37% book against 3.75% Bank Rate; PWLB break costs, for the discount position (indicative only); Treasury investment portfolio management, for the £83m LA-to-LA book; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the committee this report goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
